blocks.content: 2. Three Resources Working Together
aws_iam_role, aws_iam_policy, and aws_iam_role_policy_attachment together form the real, complete pattern for granting a specific, real identity specific, real permissions.
The role defines who or what can genuinely use it, the policy defines what real actions are actually allowed, and the attachment connects the two together.
This three-resource pattern is genuinely the most common, real way IAM permissions are granted throughout a real, live Terraform configuration.
Understanding this pattern well makes reading and writing real, correct IAM configuration considerably more straightforward.

blocks.content: 3. assume_role_policy: Who Can Use This Role
blocks.text: 3. assume_role_policy: Who Can Use This Role

blocks.content: The assume_role_policy argument determines who, or what, genuinely can actually use this role at all, a real, genuinely important, and often confusing, first step.
For a role meant to be used by an EC2 instance, this policy specifically trusts the ec2.amazonaws.com real, AWS service principal.
Getting this argument wrong is a real, common source of confusion, a role existing but genuinely unusable by the resource actually meant to assume it.
This is worth understanding clearly before writing any real, new IAM role, it is genuinely the first thing that must be correct.

blocks.alt: Who or what can genuinely use this role at all, the real, necessary first question

blocks.content: 4. A Real EC2 Instance Role Example
blocks.text: 4. A Real EC2 Instance Role Example

blocks.content: Recall Least Privilege from the Security module, a real EC2 instance role should hold exactly the specific, real permissions that instance genuinely needs, and nothing more.
An instance reading from a specific, real S3 bucket needs exactly s3:GetObject on that specific bucket's real ARN, not broad, convenient S3 access generally.
This is precisely the scoped-policy discipline already covered, applied here to a real, concrete, everyday EC2 use case.
Building this policy incrementally, exactly as already covered, keeps it genuinely reflecting only what this specific role actually, really needs.

blocks.content: 5. The Instance Profile: A Real, Necessary Bridge
blocks.text: 5. The Instance Profile: A Real, Necessary Bridge

blocks.content: An aws_iam_instance_profile is the real, necessary bridge connecting an IAM role to an actual, live EC2 instance, a genuinely easy detail to overlook.
An EC2 instance cannot reference a role directly, it references an instance profile, which itself wraps around the real, actual role.
Forgetting this bridge resource is a real, common, genuinely confusing mistake, a correctly-configured role that an instance still genuinely cannot use.
This small, real detail is worth remembering specifically, it is genuinely one of the most common points of confusion in real EC2 IAM setup.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784555876504-669064739.png
blocks.alt: A real, necessary bridge, easy to overlook, connecting a role to an actual, live instance

The aws_iam_policy_document data source, already glimpsed earlier in this topic, is a genuinely cleaner, real way to write policies than a raw, embedded JSON string.
This gives real HCL syntax, validation, and genuine composability, rather than a real, error-prone JSON string embedded directly inside a resource.
This is worth adopting as a real, practical default for writing any IAM policy, rather than hand-writing raw JSON directly.
This connects directly back to the general preference for real, structured HCL already established throughout this entire course.

Recall the scoped-policy discipline already covered in the Security module, applied again here, directly, to this real, concrete role and policy example.
Every specific action and resource named explicitly, rather than a broad, convenient wildcard, exactly the same real practice already established.
This repetition is deliberate, real, effective IAM practice is the exact same, single discipline, applied consistently, across every real role a project creates.

blocks.content: 8. A Real, Common Mistake
Attaching AdministratorAccess directly, for real, quick convenience, is a real, common, genuinely dangerous mistake, especially during early, fast-moving development.
This grants genuinely unrestricted access, far beyond whatever a specific, real role actually needs, a real violation of least privilege from the very start.
The honest fix is exactly the incremental, scoped-policy discipline already covered, real, deliberate effort worth the genuine, added security.
This mistake is worth catching immediately in any real code review, exactly the scrutiny already covered for IAM changes generally.

9. Managed Policies vs Inline Policies
AWS managed policies are real, pre-built, reusable policies, customer-managed policies are real, custom ones a team writes and genuinely maintains itself.
A real, common AWS managed policy, AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess, for instance, is convenient but genuinely broader than a real, scoped, custom policy would be.
For genuinely production-grade, real infrastructure, a custom, scoped policy, exactly the discipline already covered throughout this topic, is the honest, preferred choice.
Understanding this distinction helps explain why a real, seemingly convenient managed policy is often not the genuinely best, real, long-term choice.

The exact same role-policy-attachment pattern already covered applies directly to Lambda functions, ECS tasks, and nearly every other, real AWS compute service.
Only the assume_role_policy's real, trusted service principal genuinely changes, lambda.amazonaws.com instead of ec2.amazonaws.com, for instance.
Recognizing this consistency means everything covered in this topic transfers directly to real AWS services beyond just EC2 specifically.
This is a genuinely valuable, real, transferable pattern, worth remembering well beyond this topic's specific, EC2-focused examples.
